title: Утренняя паника Кости и Саши  (Kostya and Sasha's Morning Panic)

segments.t: Back at the apartment, Kostya and Sasha wake up horrified to discover they slept together after drinking too much the night before. Kostya grabs his phone to confess everything to Max, but Sasha pleads with him to stay quiet just as Max walks through the door.
Вернее, я не знаю, как это произошло.
Я не хочу его терять, понимаешь?
Кто не видел, что я хотел сесть встать?
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'It is none of your business where I am calling.' Max anchors the line on 'not', while 'to call' completes the thought.
'This turned out really badly.' The meaning hinges on 'worked out' working together with 'fine' in spoken Russian. Max answers right away.
Вернее, я не знаю, как это произошло.
'Or rather, I do not even know how this happened.' The grammar packs 'more accurately' and 'happened' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'Oh, hey there, Kostyan.' Kostya anchors the line on 'about', while 'Kostyan' completes the thought.
'I am calling Max right now.' In Russian, the idea of 'I' flows naturally into 'Max' without extra filler words. Kostya answers right away.
'Wait, do not call anywhere.' In Russian, the idea of 'wait' flows naturally into 'call' without extra filler words.
Я не хочу его терять, понимаешь?
'I do not want to lose him, do you understand?' The negative particle sits right before the verb meaning 'want' to negate the statement.
'Me, go to sleep?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'to sleep'. Max answers right away.
'And about football.' Max brings out the contrast between 'both' and 'about' in a few short words.
'Just shut up, I know!' Notice how Russian expresses 'yes' and 'know' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Кто не видел, что я хотел сесть встать?
'Who did not see that I wanted to sit down and stand up?' Notice how Russian expresses 'who' and 'to stand up' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Kostya answers right away.
'And so what?' The grammar packs 'both' and 'what' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'Because that is what I wanted to do!' In Russian, the idea of 'and' flows naturally into 'wanted' without extra filler words. Let's hear the full exchange one more time at natural speed.
